D_server_side_logic.additional_logic: 1. Tool annotations: No annotations were found in the official materials. One `code` tool may invoke reads and writes among authorized functions; specific read/write function inventory is not published. 2. Server-enforced confirmation: Unknown for this MCP endpoint. Rippling AI product materials say proposed Rippling AI actions require explicit human confirmation, but do not establish that this applies to external MCP clients. 3. Permissions: the server chooses functions from the connected user's policy and role before execution; Rippling says the same scopes and field-level permissions apply when calls reach its host. MCP OAuth scopes and token lifecycle are unknown. 4. Restrictions: one global endpoint was provided; no read-only mode, tool filters, URL flags, or regional variants found. Program execution is capped at 60 seconds. 5. Isolation: generated code has no credentials or network access and cannot directly access Rippling; access is limited to functions supplied for the request. Field-level permissions are enforced. No PII masking rules found. 6. Limits: edge rate limiting and abuse controls are stated, without numeric quotas; each program has a hard 60-second budget. 7. Validation/correction: typed functions are described, but unknown-argument rejection, coercion, aliasing, or operator overrides are not documented. 8. Audit/telemetry: endpoint-specific logging and telemetry unknown; separate MCP Gateway materials state calls are recorded for review. 9. Vendor-interest mechanisms: no feedback, rating, report, survey, or upsell tool identified in the published one-tool MCP list. 10. Behavior shaping: tool descriptions include capability and latency guidance; prose includes recommendations such as function ordering and parallel execution. Enforcement of text guidance is not specified. 11. Memory/state: no persistence or cross-request behavioral state documented; each program runs in a fresh isolate. 12. Structure: a single MCP tool invokes a typed internal function catalog (31 reported functions) through an isolated runtime; no nested MCP server documented. 13. Escape hatch: no raw API, arbitrary SQL, or direct network access documented; the code tool can compose the specific functions granted for its request.
behavioural_instructions_to_ai_verbatim: Which functions it gets is decided before a single line runs.
The only thing it can do is call the specific codemode.* functions we hand it for that request.

D_server_side_logic.server_structure_explanation: The MCP interface exposes one `code` tool backed by a separate typed catalog of 31 `codemode.*` functions, with model-generated programs executed in an isolated Worker. The functions are available through the code tool rather than exposed as individual MCP tools.

E_aggregated.action_count: 1 MCP tool; 31 internal typed functions reported
E_aggregated.action_count_comment: An official tool description/list exists only as described in the official engineering post: https://www.rippling.com/blog/building-mcp-server. It states one `code` MCP tool and 31 `codemode.*` functions, but does not publish the full tool schema or enumerate all 31 functions. `actions.json` therefore lists the one officially named MCP tool; internal functions are not MCP tools. StackOne reports 37 actions for its separately hosted integration; Glama lists 19 tools for the unofficial bifrost-mcp local server. Neither catalogue describes the input endpoint's tool list, so neither was added.

actions.description: Runs a JavaScript program using the connected user's authorized typed codemode.* functions; intermediate API responses remain inside an isolated Worker and the program result is returned.

F_documentation.implementation_hints_not_enforced: The engineering post describes text-based tool guidance: it reports adding p95 latency to function descriptions and instructing agents to account for sequential versus parallel calls under the 60-second ceiling. It also publishes example action-header routing guidance. These are agent-facing descriptions; the source does not say the server enforces the recommended call strategy.
F_documentation.governance_promises: The vendor says access uses the user's Rippling identity and permissions, updates when role changes, and applies field-level permissions. It says generated code has no credentials or network access, while the server applies rate limiting and a 60-second program budget. General Rippling AI materials say usage data is not used to train AI models, but this statement is not explicitly scoped to the MCP endpoint.
F_documentation.promises_to_user: Rippling markets the MCP as a governed way for external agents to use company data and tools, with up to 98% fewer tokens in its example and the ability to perform cross-domain workflows.
F_documentation.comparison_with_server_logic: User permission inheritance, field-level checks, worker isolation, rate limiting, and execution budget are described as server-side measures. The 98% token reduction is a reported comparative result. No endpoint-specific retention, audit, or AI-training implementation is documented; the no-training statement applies to Rippling AI generally.

contradictions: StackOne's page lists 37 actions for StackOne's hosted Rippling integration; Rippling's official post describes one `code` MCP tool for the input product. These are distinct server surfaces, so StackOne's actions were not included.

Glama lists 19 tools under the unofficial `bifrost-mcp/rippling-mcp` server, which uses a Rippling API token and configurable API base URL. It is not official code or evidence for the hosted endpoint's tool list; its names were not included.

The OAuth challenge references protected-resource metadata at `/mcp`, but that metadata URL and the other supplied OAuth discovery URLs returned HTTP 403 Cloudflare pages, preventing comparison of scopes with the tool/function catalog.
observations_for_research: The endpoint's advertised MCP surface is intentionally compressed to one code-execution tool, while its backend exposes a larger permission-filtered function catalog.
The vendor describes both runtime permission enforcement and agent-oriented text optimization, including latency guidance and a compact action header.
The available OAuth evidence establishes that a bearer token is required, but the discovery documents needed to characterize authorization scopes were inaccessible.
